question: to the Commission Christophe Gomart (PPE), Susana Solís Pérez (PPE), Zala Tomašič (PPE), Fernando Navarrete Rojas (PPE), François-Xavier Bellamy (PPE), Céline Imart (PPE), Isabelle Le Callennec (PPE) Subject:

The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) has delivered important protections for citizens’ personal data. However, its current interpretation regarding sole traders, who act simultaneously as individuals and business entities, is having unintended consequences. Because no distinction is made between personal and professional data, European sole traders’ business information cannot be processed by business information providers (BIPs) without significant complexity – such as conducting a legally precarious ‘legitimate interest’ balancing test or obtaining individual consent – with a wide variety of differing interpretations of the regulation across the EU. The data gap results in greater complexity or even economic exclusion of sole traders, undermining the competitiveness of European small and medium-sized enterprises in the global marketplace. In this context, can the Commission clarify: 1.
Whether it is aware of these negative effects and their impact on the functioning of the single market, competitiveness, anti-money laundering support and the cost of complexity?

What concrete steps will it take to reform GDPR enforcement, enabling proportionate and lawful processing of sole traders’ business data with a clear distinction between personal and professional data?

More generally, whether it will support BIPs through a practical, reuse-friendly framework aligned with the European Data Strategy and single market goals for fair, transparent and competitive markets?

(9 July 2026) Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)) (1) does not cover the processing of personal data concerning legal persons, such as their name, form and contact details. Nevertheless, certain information about legal persons may exceptionally constitute personal data, e.g. when the official title identifies natural persons (2). Although a sole proprietor (i.e. self-employed), carries out business activity, and is thus engaged in a form of business, a sole proprietor is owned and run by one individual (‘you are your business’). It does not constitute a separate legal entity with its own legal personality, unlike a corporation. Accordingly, it is not a company or firm (i.e. legal person) as defined by Article 54 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU (3). Personal data protection must be considered in relation to its function in society and be balanced against other fundamental rights in accordance with the principle of proportionality (4). For example, the anti-money laundering legislative package contains robust data protection safeguards, without compromising the legislative objective (5).

Regulation (EU) 2025/2518 (6) streamlines GDPR enforcement in cross-border cases. To achieve the consistent application of the GDPR, the European Data Protection Board has committed to facilitating easier GDPR compliance, including by providing ready-to-use templates (7), as also called for by the Commission (8). The GDPR implementation dialogue, which took place in July 2025, reaffirmed that the GDPR is a balanced legal framework and has met its objectives (9). Nevertheless, to boost competitiveness, increase legal certainty, reduce costs and strengthen enforcement, targeted amendments to the GDPR are proposed in the Digital Omnibus (10).
